title: Working with data
text:
Course overview
This book is a work-in-progress intended to support the course MGMT2605 - Working with Data offered at the Faculty of Management of Dalhousie University. The course introduces this knowledge and skillset through lectures and hands-on labs. Students will learn to use a variety of tools to find, manage, assess, extract value from, and visualize raw data.

title: Working with data
text:
Learning outcomes
Upon completion of this course, students should be able to:

Manipulate, assess, analyze, and share raw data of different types (including quantitative data, qualitative data, and GIS data)
Identify the nature and extent of data needed and collected for given managerial purposes
Locate, collect, and integrate data of multiple types from multiple sources
Use data to inform evidence-based decision-making
Understand the data lifecycle (including collection, management, analysis, and application)
Demonstrate critical evaluation at various stages of the data lifecycle
Assess data visualizations and analyses for accuracy, relevance, and objectivity
Employ a range of data skills to address diverse, real-world scenarios/problems in multiple sectors and disciplines
Use data ethically and with awareness of the capabilities and limitations of data analysis

title: 1  What is data?
text:
1.1 Data
The Merriam-Webster online dictionary provides three definitions of the word data:
Together, these definitions offer us a set of key elements from which we can build a broad understanding of the concept of data. The first key term is factual information or fact suggesting that data is objective and, like the rest of the definition shows, is used for a given purpose, such as discussing reasoning or decision-making.
The second definition is related to using the word data in a computational or communicational sense, where data is the “thing” that is being stored, transmitted, received, processed, etc.
While the first definition suggests that humans and machines use data for processes such as decisions and calculations, the third definition highlights that data does not only exist in nature but can also be created by humans and machines, either purposefully or not.
While we often think of data as things found in spreadsheets and stored in computers or filing cabinets, data is much more than that. Data is everywhere around us all the time in the form of energy and sound or light waves, for instance. Our sensory organs are data captors that pick up data from our environment. Our brains process, structure, and possibly store the data so we can consciously or unconsciously use it now or later as a basis for decisions and actions. That said, in this course, we will not concern ourselves with this kind of data and process. Instead, we will focus on digitally recorded data, the kind that we can store in a computer.
One way to try to make sense of the concept of data is by situating it in relation to other concepts. The data, information, knowledge and wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy or pyramid (pictured below) can be helpful to us as it offers a visual representation of such a relationship.
The pyramid suggests that data generates information, information generates knowledge, and knowledge generates wisdom. However, there is no consensus on the definition of each level of the pyramid, no consensus regarding the number of layers the pyramid should have, and no consensus regarding the hierarchical nature of the relationship between the concepts (Rowley 2007). Couldn’t we capture knowledge and store it in the form of data, for example?
Rowley (2007) reviewed the literature on the pyramid and found that data is typically understood as discrete objects, facts or observations, or recorded descriptions of things, events, activities, or transactions.

title: 1  What is data?
text:
1.2 Datasets
We often encounter the term “dataset” on the web or in our workplaces, and I think it is worth writing a few lines to relate the terms to the other terms we will use in this course. The terms data and dataset will often be used interchangeably since dataset literally means a set of data, and data is the plural of datum. One difference, in principle, is that datasets are usually assembled for a given purpose. In research, for instance, a dataset will be the exact collection of data collected for the analysis. In supervised machine learning, we distinguish between training and testing datasets. When a professor sends you an excel file with data to work with for an assignment, that’s a dataset. You find datasets when you browse websites like kaggle.com, zenodo.org, or dataverse.org. Datasets are also static, whereas databases can be dynamic.

title: 1  What is data?
text:
1.3 Databases
What is a database? According to the Merriam-Webster dictionary, a database is “a usually large collection of data organized especially for rapid search and retrieval (as by a computer)”. The keyword here is organized, highlighting that databases are both products and tools for data management.
Databases are usually created and managed for some purposes. These purposes may be specific (e.g. keeping track of a store’s inventory) or broad (tracking socioeconomic trends). Depending on their purposes, databases can vary in size and complexity. Any organized data collection could be considered a database, even if it is as basic as an Excel spreadsheet with the names and addresses of your friends or your to-do list.
A database can contain or be used to create multiple datasets, but a dataset would typically not contain multiple databases. Of course, this does not mean that datasets are always drawn from databases. For example, datasets can be created by surveying or interviewing people or recording observations of natural phenomena.
Note, however, that those differences are not hard truths, as some datasets may serve a greater variety of users and purposes than some databases.

1.4 Database management systems (DBMS)
A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that supports the development, maintenance, security, and use of databases. You will often come across the DBMS acronym with different suffixes attached to it, such as RDBMS (Relational DBMS), OODBMS (Object-Oriented DBMS), or ORDBMS (Object-Relational DBMS). Note that all these DBMS generally offer the same basic features. The main difference is that they work with different data types and structures. You will not working with a DBMS in this course but we will mention some of the most popular ones that work with the specific data structures that we encounter.

title: 1  What is data?
text:
1.5 Data management
So far in this chapter, we explored the concepts of data and its different levels of structure, datasets, databases and data management systems. Aside from related to data, what do all these concepts have in common? They are what data managers work with. Data managers unlock the potential of data for a given purpose, individual, group or organization, by developing and implementing data strategies and processes such as data retrieval, processing, cleaning, storage and analysis.
The value of data depends on the purpose it serves. Thus, good data management requires a good understanding of both the data and the needs of its users so that optimal data strategies can be developed and implemented.

From unstructured to structured data
Data can take many forms that we can situate along a continuum with unstructured data at one extreme, structured data at the other, and semi-structured data in between. In this section, we briefly explore what these concepts mean.

title: Data structures
Data structures
text:
The power of structure
The more structured a dataset is, the more easily it will be to use to extract knowledge by an end-user. Unfortunately, data is not always found in easily exploitable structures and will often require some cleaning and processing. There is a well-known saying that data scientists spend 80% of their time cleaning their data. Clean data that fits a clear purpose is actually extremely easy to analyze… the problem is that the purpose isn’t always clear in the end of the user, and data does not always come in the exact format needed for that purpose.

title: Data structures
text:
the JSON structure
A JSON file is nothing more than a text file that contains text that follows the JSON syntax. So we can create them with any text editor (e.g. notepad, MS Word, Google Doc). A JSON file must always begin with and end with a curly bracket {}.

Key-value pairs
In JSON, everything is a key-value pair except for objects and arrays for which the key is optional. The key is always between double quotes, and so are values that are strings. Here’s an example of a key-value pair.

"name":"Barry Bonds"

Here “name” is the key, and “Barry Bonds” is the value. This data is the equivalent of an spreadsheet that looks like this:
So a JSON file with only that one key-value pair would look like this:

{ 
  "name":"Barry Bonds"
} 



Types of values in JSON
In JSON, values must be one of the following data types:

String: “name” : “bada booms”
Number: “number_of_children” : 10
Boolean: “sale” : true
NULL: “middlename” : null
Object: {“name” : “John”, “age” : 30, “city” : “New York”}
Array: [“John”, “Anna”, “Peter”]



Creating a JSON object
Here’s an example of a fictional course written as a JSON, which is an example of a JSON object that could be part of a JSON collection.

{
  "code": "INFO6540",
  "semester": "Winter",
  "year": 2023,
  "description": "This is the course description",
  "brightspace_active": true,
  "students": ["Wayne Gretzky","Mario Lemieux"],
  "supplementary_files_url": null
}

And here is another course.

{
  "code": "INFO6270",
  "semester": "Fall",
  "year": 2022,
  "name": "Singing for dummies",
  "description": "This the course description for INFO6270",
  "brightspace_active": false,
  "room": "ROWE1234",
  "students": ["Justin Bieber","Lady Gaga"],
  "supplementary_files_url": "www.info6270_sup.ca"

we can see that the document contains strings (code, semester, description), numbers (year), booleans (brightspace_active), and an array (students) that contain objects.


Creating a collection (JSON array)
A collection is essentially a group of objects in an array. For example, if we wanted to store all our courses together into a collection of courses, we could do it in a single JSON file that contains an array called “courses”, like this:

title: 4  Finding and retrieving data
text:
4.1 Start with the business question
Data analytics begins before a spreadsheet is opened or a statistical model is selected. The first practical challenge is to determine what data are needed, where those data might exist, and how they can be retrieved in a form suitable for analysis. This is an important shift in perspective. Analytics is not simply a matter of receiving a ready-made file and calculating something from it. Analysts frequently have to translate a business question into data requirements, locate one or more appropriate sources, understand how those sources are structured, and decide how to obtain the relevant observations.
The search for data should begin with the managerial question rather than with a desire to find an interesting dataset. Suppose a company wants to decide where to open a coffee shop in Nova Scotia. The question immediately suggests several kinds of evidence: population and population growth, household income, employment patterns, business locations, commuting patterns, and perhaps information about existing competitors. No single source is guaranteed to contain everything required. The analyst may therefore need to combine internal organizational data with government statistics, open data, commercial or research data, and other sources.
This chapter introduces some categories of data sources and practical strategies for finding and retrieving them. It also emphasizes a distinction that will recur throughout analytics: finding a source about the right topic is not the same as finding data with the right observations, variables, geography, time period, and level of detail. Successful retrieval begins with a carefully defined need.
Before searching the web or opening an organizational database, identify the decision or question that the data are expected to support. A broad question such as “Why are sales declining?” needs to be translated into potential measures. Useful internal variables might include transactions, product categories, prices, promotions, customer segments, store locations, returns, or inventory availability. External data might include population change, inflation, weather, competitor activity, or broader economic indicators. The particular list depends on the business context.
This translation produces search concepts. A question about whether population growth is associated with housing prices in Halifax might require housing prices, population, geography, and a time variable. Those concepts are more useful for data discovery than typing the entire explanatory question into a web search engine. Searching for “Halifax housing prices dataset,” “Nova Scotia housing prices CSV,” or “Halifax population Statistics Canada” is more likely to surface downloadable data than asking a search engine why prices are increasing.
It is also important to determine what is the intended unit of observation. Will one row represent a customer, transaction, business, community, province, month, or year? This decision helps determine whether a candidate source has sufficient granularity. A provincial annual population series may be authoritative and accurate but still be irrelevant when the decision requires neighbourhood-level comparisons.

title: 5  Assessing and cleaning data
text:
5.1 Assessing data with the CRAAP test
In data analytics, finding a dataset is not the same as finding a dataset that deserves to be analyzed. A file can open perfectly in Excel, contain thousands of rows, and appear rich in information while still being unsuitable for the managerial question at hand. Its observations may be too old, its variables may not correspond to the concepts we want to study, its origin may be unclear, its measures may be poorly documented, or the data may have been collected for a purpose that limits the conclusions we can reasonably draw. For this reason, evaluating a dataset should happen before significant effort is invested in cleaning, transforming, visualizing, or modelling it.
The CRAAP Test provides a memorable structure for doing this evaluation. Developed as an information-evaluation tool at Meriam Library, California State University, Chico, the framework asks users to consider five dimensions: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, and Purpose. The original guidance treats these criteria as questions for evaluating information sources and explicitly notes that the relative importance of the criteria depends on the information need. In a data analytics course, the same five ideas can be adapted to datasets by focusing on when the observations were collected, whether the dataset fits the business question, who produced it, how its measurements were generated and documented, and why the data were collected in the first place.

title: 5  Assessing and cleaning data
text:
5.1.1 Currency: Are the data timely enough?
Currency refers to the timeliness of information. The original CRAAP guidance asks when information was published or posted, whether it has been revised or updated, and whether the topic requires current information or whether older material will work. Applied to data, the first question should normally be even more specific: when were the observations actually collected? A dataset can be downloaded today while describing conditions from many years ago. The date on a webpage or file therefore does not necessarily tell us the period represented by the data. 
For a management problem, currency should be evaluated relative to the decision rather than according to a universal rule that newer is always better. Imagine a manager deciding where to open a new retail location. Population figures from a much earlier census may accurately describe that historical period, but they may provide weak evidence about the current size and composition of a fast-changing community. In contrast, if the analytical question concerns how a market changed over the previous decade, older observations are not a defect: they are essential evidence. The important question is whether the temporal coverage of the dataset matches the temporal scope of the question. 
It is helpful to identify at least three different dates where possible:

the period during which observations were collected
the date on which the dataset was released
the date on which it was most recently updated.

It is also helpful to ask whether the source is updated periodically. A dataset that is refreshed regularly may be useful for recurring managerial decisions, while a one-time survey may be appropriate for a particular analysis but unsuitable for monitoring change over time. 


5.1.2 Relevance: Do the data fit the business question? 
Relevance is the importance of information for a particular need. In the original CRAAP framework, users are asked whether information relates to the topic or answers the question and whether it is appropriate for the intended audience and purpose. For datasets, relevance becomes a concrete exercise in matching a business question to the structure and coverage of the data. 
A useful dataset should contain the right population or market, geography, time period, variables, and unit of observation. The unit of observation is especially important. It describes what one row represents. A row might represent an individual customer, a transaction, a company, a neighbourhood, a province, or a month. Two datasets can concern exactly the same topic while supporting very different analyses because their units of observation differ. 
Consider the question: “Where should a company open a new coffee shop in Nova Scotia?” A provincial table containing Nova Scotia’s total population is related to the topic, but it is unlikely to be sufficiently granular for choosing among locations. A community-level dataset would be more relevant. Useful variables might include population, population growth, household income, business locations, commuting patterns, or other indicators justified by the proposed decision. A variable may be interesting without being analytically necessary. Relevance means asking what the business question requires, not collecting every field that happens to be available. 
The same principle applies when assessing a dataset title or description. A dataset labelled “Halifax Housing Data” may sound ideal for a question about housing prices, but closer inspection might reveal that each row represents an annual provincial average rather than an individual sale or neighbourhood. Alternatively, it might contain property characteristics without any price variable. The dataset is topically related yet analytically inadequate. 
Before downloading a large file, it is helpful to inspect its documentation, preview, variable list, or data dictionary and ask: What does each row represent? Which variables are present? What population is included? What geography is available? Which years are covered? Answering those questions often eliminates unsuitable datasets before time is spent cleaning them. 


5.1.3 Authority: Who is responsible for the data? 
Authority concerns the source of information. The original CRAAP guidance asks who the author, publisher, source, or sponsor is; what qualifications or affiliations they have; and whether they are qualified to provide information on the subject. For a dataset, authority is closely connected to provenance: being able to trace where the data came from and who was responsible for collecting, processing, or publishing them. 
This matters because a spreadsheet generally does not carry its credibility inside its cells. Imagine two files containing similar population figures. One is published by an identified statistical agency and accompanied by definitions and methodological documentation. The other is called “population.csv” and was uploaded by an unknown account with no explanation. Even if some numbers are identical, the analyst has a very different basis for judging the two files. With the first, the analyst can examine provenance and documentation. With the second, fundamental questions about origin may remain unanswered. 
Authority should not be reduced to the claim that government, academic, or corporate sources are automatically correct. Instead, ask whether the producer is identifiable and whether the producer has an appropriate basis for creating the dataset. A retailer may be authoritative about its own sales transactions. A statistical agency may have responsibility and expertise for official socioeconomic statistics. A market-research company may provide useful commercial data but require the analyst to understand its methodology and coverage. Authority gives us a starting point for evaluating responsibility and expertise, not a substitute for examining the data themselves. 
Useful evidence of authority includes a clearly identified publisher or data owner, documentation explaining responsibility for the dataset, contact information, metadata, and an identifiable organizational context. When provenance cannot be established, that uncertainty itself becomes a limitation that should be documented before the data are used. 


5.1.4 Accuracy: How were the values produced? 
In the original CRAAP framework, Accuracy concerns reliability, truthfulness, and correctness. The guidance asks where the information comes from, whether it is supported by evidence, whether it has been reviewed, and whether it can be verified against another source. For datasets, accuracy assessment begins by asking how observations and variables were produced and what the values actually mean. 
Good data documentation can be as important as the data values. Analysts should look for the collection methodology, variable definitions, units of measurement, coding conventions, sampling information where applicable, and metadata describing the dataset. Without this information, even apparently simple numbers can be ambiguous. A field labelled “Income” with the value 72, for example, is uninterpretable without context. Does 72 mean $72, $72,000, monthly income, annual income, individual income, or household income? A technically clean column can remain conceptually unusable. 
Accuracy also involves examining whether important values can be checked. This does not mean manually validating every observation. It means asking whether the source explains how values were generated and whether key figures or patterns can be compared with credible benchmarks when appropriate. Documentation may also reveal estimation, suppression, rounding, sampling, or other characteristics that affect interpretation. 
It is easy to confuse accuracy assessment with data cleaning. Some issues do overlap, but the distinction is important. If one date appears as “2026-03-01” and another as “03/01/2026,” the analyst has a formatting and cleaning problem. If the analyst does not know whether a date column represents transaction date, reporting date, or data-entry date, the problem is one of definition and documentation. Standardizing the format cannot solve uncertainty about what the variable signifies. 
This distinction reinforces a broader lesson: cleaning improves the consistency of the representation of data; it does not establish that the underlying observations are valid measures of what the analyst intends to study. 


5.1.5 Purpose: Why were the data collected? 
Purpose is the reason information exists. The original CRAAP guidance asks whether a source is intended to inform, teach, sell, entertain, or persuade, whether the source makes its intentions clear, and whether a point of view or bias may affect the information. For datasets, the parallel question is: Why were these observations collected in the first place? 
Data may be collected for administration, service delivery, billing, regulatory reporting, research, marketing, public information, advocacy, or many other reasons. The original purpose shapes what variables are captured and how they are defined. A gym’s membership system, for example, may contain excellent information about membership type, payment status, visits, and cancellations because those fields support routine operations. The same database may contain little information about why members value the gym because understanding attitudes was not the system’s operational purpose. 
Purpose therefore helps analysts understand both strengths and absences. A dataset created for billing may have precise payment records but limited behavioural context. A survey created to study customer satisfaction may contain detailed attitudes but rely on responses from only those who participated. Neither purpose automatically makes the data good or bad. The point is to consider how the collection purpose may influence what was measured, what was omitted, how categories were created, and what conclusions the dataset can support. 
It is also helpful to consider whether their proposed analytical use is compatible with the evidence present in the dataset. Data often become attractive simply because they are available. The CRAAP framework encourages the analyst to reverse that logic: begin with the decision and evaluate whether the source was produced in a way that makes it suitable evidence for that decision. 


5.1.6 CRAAP assessment is not data cleaning 
The distinction between dataset assessment and dataset cleaning is one of the most important lessons in an introductory analytics course. CRAAP asks, “Should we use this dataset for this question?” Data cleaning asks, “What must we standardize, correct, reshape, or document before we analyze the dataset?” 
Typical cleaning issues include duplicate records, inconsistent category labels, missing values, leading or trailing spaces, dates represented in multiple formats, and numbers stored as text. These are important technical problems. But successfully fixing them does not answer questions about currency, relevance, provenance, methodology, or purpose. You can spend an hour producing an immaculate spreadsheet that still cannot answer the managerial question. 
Conversely, CRAAP assessment does not mean that a suitable dataset will be clean. An authoritative and highly relevant administrative dataset may contain awkward codes, structural blanks, duplicated exports, or hierarchical fields that require substantial transformation. Dataset assessment and cleaning are complementary rather than competing processes. Evaluation determines whether the source deserves further investment; cleaning prepares an accepted source for analysis. 


5.1.7 Using CRAAP in the analytics workflow 
For a management analytics project, CRAAP fits naturally between finding a candidate source and retrieving it for detailed work. A practical sequence is: define the business question; identify the observations and variables that would answer it; search for candidate datasets; apply the CRAAP criteria; decide whether the evidence is suitable; then retrieve, clean, analyze, and communicate the results. 
This ordering prevents a common inefficiency. We often download the first promising file we find, spend substantial effort repairing columns and formats, and only later discover that the file covers the wrong period, geography, population, or unit of observation. A short evaluation at the beginning can prevent extensive work on data that were never suitable. 
The process is also iterative. A CRAAP review may reveal that one dataset is useful for population but lacks business-location information. Rather than rejecting it entirely, an analyst might retain it as one component of a multi-source analysis and search for another authoritative dataset that fills the missing requirement. Evaluation therefore supports thoughtful source combination as well as source rejection. 
The CRAAP Test gives beginning analysts a straightforward vocabulary for asking difficult but necessary questions about evidence. Currency asks whether the observations are timely enough. Relevance asks whether the dataset fits the population, geography, period, variables, and unit of observation required by the question. Authority asks who stands behind the data. Accuracy asks how the values were produced, defined, documented, and verified. Purpose asks why the observations were collected and how that purpose may shape what the dataset can tell us. 
The central lesson is that data quality cannot be reduced to tidy rows and columns. Before analysts worry about duplicates, formatting, formulas, charts, or models, they should establish that the dataset is a defensible source of evidence for the decision being made. CRAAP provides a practical checkpoint: evaluate first, clean second, analyze third. 
The habit to develop is simple: when a promising file appears in a search result, resist the urge to download immediately. Ask what period it represents, whether its structure matches the question, who created it, how its measurements were produced, and why those measurements exist. Then make an explicit decision: use the dataset, use it while acknowledging limitations, or keep searching. That judgment is not separate from analytics. It is one of the first analytical decisions a manager or analyst makes.

title: 5  Assessing and cleaning data
text:
5.2 Cleaning data
Finding and evaluating a dataset are only the beginning of an analytics project. Once an analyst has decided that a dataset is sufficiently relevant and credible for a business question, the next task is to make the data usable. Real organizational data rarely arrive as a perfectly structured table with consistent categories, complete observations, correct data types, and one unambiguous record for every entity. Instead, analysts encounter duplicated records, blank cells, inconsistent spelling and capitalization, multiple date formats, numbers stored as text, impossible values, and variables whose structure does not match the analysis they want to perform. 
Data cleaning is the systematic process of identifying and addressing these kinds of problems before analysis. IBM describes data cleaning as identifying and correcting errors and inconsistencies in raw datasets so that the data are more accurate, complete, consistent, and usable for analysis or decision-making. Common problems include duplicates, missing values, inconsistencies, syntax errors, irrelevant data, and structural errors. This definition is useful because it emphasizes that cleaning is not cosmetic. The objective is not a prettier spreadsheet. The objective is a dataset whose structure and values can support dependable analysis. 
At the same time, cleaning requires judgment. Not every unusual value is an error, not every blank should be filled, and not every repeated observation is a duplicate. An analyst who mechanically “fixes” everything that looks unusual can damage valid information. Good data cleaning therefore combines technical operations with an understanding of what each row and variable mean. 

5.2.1 Begin by understanding the structure of the data 
Before changing anything, the analyst should understand the dataset as it currently exists. Start with the unit of observation: what does one row represent? A row may represent a customer, a transaction, a product, a gym visit, a month, or a geographic area. Next identify what each column represents and what type of value should appear there. This step sounds simple, but many cleaning decisions depend on it. 
Consider the Harbour Fitness exercise used in class. If each row represents a gym member, then CustomerID should identify a member, MembershipType should contain a membership category, VisitsLast30Days should represent a count, and CancellationDate should contain a date only when a cancellation has occurred. Once the intended structure is clear, potential problems become easier to distinguish from legitimate variation. 
A first inspection should look for unexpected blanks, repeated identifiers, surprising minimum or maximum values, inconsistent category names, and columns whose apparent data type does not match their meaning. The goal is diagnosis, not immediate correction. Keeping an untouched copy of the raw data is a sound classroom and workplace habit because it preserves the original evidence and makes cleaning decisions traceable. 


5.2.2 Duplicates: repeated data are not always duplicate data 
Duplicate records are a common cleaning issue. IBM includes duplicate records among typical forms of dirty data, and Microsoft Power Query provides transformations for identifying, keeping, and removing duplicate rows. Microsoft also notes that duplicate comparison in Power Query is case-sensitive, an important detail when categories differ only in capitalization. 
The central question is not simply “Does this value appear twice?” but “Should these rows represent one observation or two?” Two customers may have the same name. Two transactions may have the same amount. Neither situation necessarily represents duplication. By contrast, if every field in two member records is identical because the same export row was appended twice, the analyst may have good reason to treat one as an accidental duplicate. 
A first step is to identify the fields that establish uniqueness. In a customer file, CustomerID may be more informative than customer name. In a transaction file, a transaction identifier may be required. If no reliable key exists, duplicate detection becomes a substantive judgment based on combinations of fields and business knowledge. 
Order also matters. If “Nova Scotia” and “nova scotia” are intended to be the same value, case differences can prevent otherwise identical rows from matching. Microsoft explicitly warns that Power Query is case-sensitive when working with duplicates and suggests applying an uppercase or lowercase transformation first when case should not matter. This illustrates why cleaning should be planned as a sequence rather than as a random list of fixes. 


5.2.3 Standardizing text and categories 
Categorical variables often contain several textual representations of the same concept. A membership field may contain “Monthly,” “monthly,” and “MONTHLY.” A province could appear as “NS,” “ns,” “N.S.,” or “Nova Scotia.” If those differences are not meaningful, software may treat them as separate categories, producing misleading counts and fragmented summaries. 
Standardization means choosing a consistent representation for values that are known to mean the same thing. The analyst might map all legitimate Nova Scotia variants to “NS,” all monthly membership variants to “Monthly,” and Y/Yes/yes to “Yes.” The important phrase is “known to mean the same thing.” Standardization should be based on semantics, documentation, or business rules rather than visual similarity alone. 
Text also frequently contains leading or trailing spaces or inconsistent capitalization. These problems can be difficult to see while still interfering with joins, filtering, grouping, and duplicate detection. Cleaning text may therefore include trimming unnecessary spaces and applying a consistent case convention. Names require particular care, because automated capitalization rules can produce incorrect results for legitimate names. A useful teaching principle is that automation should standardize what is genuinely standardized and flag what requires review. 


5.2.4 Missing values: blank does not always mean missing 
Missing data are often introduced as empty cells, but an empty cell can have several meanings. It may represent information that was not collected, a value that is unknown, a value that does not apply, or a data-entry or import problem. Treating these situations as equivalent can distort an analysis. 
The Harbour Fitness dataset provides a useful example. For a member whose MembershipStatus is Active, a blank CancellationDate and CancellationReason are structurally appropriate: the member has not cancelled. Those cells should not be “fixed” by inserting a date or a cancellation reason. By contrast, a Cancelled member whose CancellationDate is blank may have genuinely missing information that requires investigation. The visible symptom is the same, a blank cell, but the meaning is different. 
This distinction leads to an important rule: do not impute or replace missing values simply because an Excel cell is empty. First determine what the blank signifies. Depending on the context, an analyst may leave missing values as missing, retrieve the information from another source, exclude affected observations from a particular analysis, create an explicit category such as “Unknown” when conceptually appropriate, or apply a justified statistical imputation method. The correct approach depends on why the information is missing and how the variable will be used. 
A second important distinction is between zero and missing. Zero is a value. Blank means the value is absent or not recorded unless documentation says otherwise. Replacing an unknown number of gym visits with zero asserts that the member made no visits. That assertion requires evidence. 


5.2.5 Data types and formats 
A value can look correct to a person while being stored incorrectly for analysis. A monthly fee displayed as “$59.99” might be text rather than a numeric value. A date might be a recognizable string rather than an Excel date. A customer identifier composed of digits may be an identifier, not a number on which arithmetic makes sense. 
Cleaning therefore includes assigning appropriate data types. Numeric measures should normally be stored as numeric values if they will be calculated or summarized. Dates should be represented consistently as actual dates when time-based analysis is required. Text categories should remain text. Identifiers should preserve their intended representation, including leading zeros when those zeros are part of the identifier. 
Mixed date representations are particularly instructive: “2026-03-10,” “03/10/2026,” and “Mar 10 2026” may refer to the same day, but ambiguous regional formats can also lead to misinterpretation. The analyst should first establish what the source convention means, convert valid values into a true date type, and then apply a consistent display format. Changing how a date looks is not the same as correcting an incorrectly interpreted date. 


5.2.6 Invalid, impossible, and suspicious values 
Cleaning also involves finding values that violate known rules. Some invalid values are easy to recognize: negative quantities in a field that cannot logically be negative, impossible dates, or text in a numeric field. Others require domain knowledge. A value of 200 might be impossible for age but unremarkable for monthly sales. 
Range checks and business rules are useful because consistency alone cannot reveal all errors. If MembershipStatus is “Active” but CancellationDate contains a recent date, the row may violate the logical relationship among variables even though every individual cell has a valid format. Similarly, an annual membership fee recorded as $6.99 might be numerically valid but suspicious relative to known pricing rules. 
Suspicious does not mean wrong. Outliers are especially important here. A very large sales transaction may represent an error, or it may be the most important transaction in the dataset. Analysts should investigate unusual observations before deleting or replacing them. Cleaning should preserve legitimate variation rather than force the data to look ordinary. 


5.2.7 Reshaping data for analysis 
Not every cleaning problem is a bad value. Sometimes the structure is inconvenient. Information may be embedded in a JSON hierarchy, several variables may be combined in one column, or repeated measurements may be spread across many columns when the intended analysis requires one observation per row. Preparing data can therefore involve splitting, merging, expanding, pivoting, or unpivoting fields. 
The objective should be tied to the analytical unit of observation. If a JSON customer record contains a list of purchases, flattening the structure may create one row per customer-purchase combination, repeating customer information across purchase rows. That is appropriate when the analysis concerns transactions, but not necessarily when the analysis requires one row per customer. Reshaping is therefore a conceptual decision as much as a technical operation. 
When data come from multiple sources, consistency becomes especially important. IBM notes that individually valid sources may still need processing when combined because fields can use different units or representations. Before merging datasets, analysts should verify that keys, categories, units, geographic definitions, and time periods are compatible. 


5.2.8 Documenting the cleaning process 
A cleaned dataset should not become a mysterious replacement for the raw data. Good practice is to preserve the source, document transformations, and make important decisions reproducible. A simple cleaning log can identify the field, the problem found, the action taken, and the reason for the action. 
For example, a data cleaning log might state that province variants “NS,” “ns,” “N.S.,” and “Nova Scotia” were standardized to “NS” because they refer to the same province.
Documentation is particularly valuable when cleaning requires judgment. It allows another analyst, instructor, manager, or future version of the same analyst to understand why a transformation was made. It also makes limitations explicit instead of silently hiding uncertainty. 


5.2.9 A practical cleaning workflow 
For an introductory management analytics course, data cleaning can be organized into a manageable sequence. The precise order will vary by dataset, but the following workflow encourages deliberate decisions rather than ad hoc editing: 

Preserve an untouched copy of the source data. 



Identify the unit of observation and understand every important variable. 



Inspect data types, categories, blanks, duplicates, ranges, and obvious structural problems. 



Standardize text, categories, units, and data types when equivalence is known. 



Investigate duplicates using the fields that establish uniqueness. 



Distinguish structural blanks from genuinely missing data before deciding how to handle them. 



Check business rules and relationships among variables for invalid or suspicious values. 



Reshape the table if the current structure does not match the intended analysis. 



Document transformations and unresolved limitations. 



Inspect the cleaned result before beginning analysis. 

This workflow is intentionally conservative. The objective is not to maximize the number of changes. It is to make only the changes that can be justified. A good cleaning decision should be explainable in plain language: what problem was identified, what was changed, and why the change preserves or improves the meaning of the data. 
Data cleaning is not a preliminary chore that can be separated from analytical thinking. It is the process of making raw observations consistent and usable while protecting their meaning. The analyst must recognize duplicates without deleting legitimate repetition, standardize categories without collapsing meaningful differences, handle blanks without inventing information, convert data types without misinterpreting values, investigate anomalies without automatically removing them, and reshape data in a way that matches the intended unit of analysis. 
A useful approach is to treat every cleaning operation as a claim. Replacing “N.S.” with “NS” claims that the two labels mean the same thing. Removing a row claims that it does not represent a distinct observation. Replacing a blank with zero claims that the true value is zero. Converting a date claims that its original representation has been interpreted correctly. Each claim should be supported by evidence, documentation, or a defensible business rule. 
The broader analytics sequence is therefore: define the business question, find candidate data, evaluate the source, retrieve the data, clean and transform the observations, analyze them, and communicate the result. The CRAAP Test helps decide whether the dataset deserves to enter that process. Data cleaning then ensures that the accepted dataset is represented in a form that supports analysis. Neither stage can substitute for the other.

However, life is not always that easy, and sometimes you need to look up information about a particular entry in your dataset in another dataset with a different structure. Take the following two tables, for example.

We have on the one hand a table of grades that students received in three different courses, and on the other end a table of course details. If we want to determine, for example, the average grade in Fall or Winter semester course, we need to bring these columns into the grades dataset. In the section below, you will learn how to use the VLOOKUP function to perform this task.

6.3.3.1 The VLOOKUP() function.
The VLOOPKUP() function can be used to combine the columns of two datasets that do not necessarily share the same structure. It looks like this:
=VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, column, col_index_num, [range_lookup])

The lookup value can be a single value, like “MGMT1001” or the coordinates of a cell that contains the value like B2.
The table array is the group of rows and columns (the range) in which you want to look for the lookup value. In the example above, the range would be A2:E5, A2 being the upper left corner of the range (we don’t need to include the column names), and E5 the bottom right corner of the range. However, you should always make sure that every element of your range coordinates is preceded with a dollar sign, like this: $G$2:$J$5 This fixes the range to ensure that it is not automatically modified when you copy and paste your formula to look up different values.
The column index number is the number of the column in the table array that contain the values you want to bring into the other dataset. For example, in the range above, the value I’m interested in is the third column of the range, so 3 is the value I need to include in this part of the formula.
The range lookup can take two values: TRUE or FALSE. For the purpose of this course, you should always use FALSE. TRUE is used when you want to determine whether the lookup value falls within a range of values in the table array (e.g., look up if 92 is between 90 and 100 and is a A+).

Putting it all together, what we get =VLOOKUP(B2,$G$2:$J$5,3,FALSE).

While there is rarely a single best way to visualize a specific variable, there is also usually not so many options that make sense. Your main constraint is the type of data that you are working with, so that is the first question you have to answer before thinking about how it can be visualized. In fact, these are the exact same questions that you had to ask yourself in Chapter 7 and Chapter 8, where you learned to identify and summarize categorical and numerical data. 12.2 Choosing the right visualization for your data
Just like in the previous chapter, the choices available to you for visualizing the relationship between two or more variables are are strictly determined by the type of data your are working with. Basically, there are three possible combinations

Two or more categorical variables
Two or more numerical variables
A combination of categorical and numerical variables

Here we treat timelines as a case of their own, so that would make four different possibilities.
The section below provides examples of visualizations and at the end of the chapter you will find a series of video demonstration how to produce these graphs in Excel.

12.2.1 Two categorical variables
When you have two categorical variables, the process is very similar as for single categorical variables. We need to create a contigency table, as we have learned in Chapter 7, and then we have a series of choices available to us.

12.2.1.1 Side-by-side bars
The side-by-side bars have the benefit of being very clear and allow us to display the data label (this should be avoided, however, when there are two many bars and the numbers start getting to close to each other or overlapping. However, side-by-side bars can be less space efficient than stacked bars (see below) when dealing with categories with many groups.



12.2.1.2 Stacked bars
Stacking the bars can a nice option also. These graphs are more space efficient, but the data labels can be harder to read. The labels can also get crowded and start overlapping when categories have small number of observations.
One issue with stacked bars when we do not use data labels is that it becomes difficult to see which differences between the size of two bars that are on top of the others (in this case the difference between male passengers in the first and second classes would be hard to see if the number was not included).



12.2.1.3 100% stacked bars
100% stacked bars actually allow you to reshape the bars by shaping them based on percentages, while still allowing you to show the count as the data label (unless you are working with aggregated data already in the form of percentages, then the data label would also show percentages).



12.2.1.4 Adding a third variable
Sometimes, you may wish to add a third categorical variable in the mix. This is possible, as in the example below showing, for each passenger class, the number of passenger of each sex that survived or died.

Here again, we can use stacked bars, however we can see that in some cases the numbers are small and overlap with the axes and are a bit harder to read. This is still a nice way to visualize the relationship between the three categorical variables (sex, survived, and passenger class).




12.2.2 Two numerical variables
The go to graph when dealing with two numerical variables is the scatterplot, which displays each observation as a dot on the graph situated at coordinates determined by the two numerical variables. In the example below, we plotted the relationship between age and ticket fare. We also added a linear trend line and the R2 to help determine the direction and strength of the relationship between the two. Since the red line has a positive slope (it goes up as age and ticket fare increase, we can quickly see that the relationship is positive, and the low R2 value of 0.0318 tells confirms that the relationship is not strong. This is generally teh case when the dots do not seem to follow a regular pattern and are scattered all over and away from the trend line.



12.2.3 A numerical and a categorical variables
When dealing with a numerical and a categorical variables, we have two choices… we can produce a panel of histograms (one for each possible value of the categorical variable) or make a graph with multiple box plots (one for each value of the categorical variable).
The example below show a panel of three histograms (one for each passenger class) with the age distribution of Titanic passengers. This works pretty well, although it’s hard to see if there is a difference between the distribution for the second and third class. Another issue is that if that if we are working with a categorical variable with a lot of possible values, the amount of space needed to visualize each distribution may quickly become an issue.

The two problems with histogram panels (the amount of space they take and the challenge in seeing differences) make the series of box plots an interesting alternative. As you can see, the example below is much more space efficient, and we can clearly see that the third class passengers tend to be younger then the second class passengers, who tend to be significantly younger than first class passengers. While they may not be the most popular visualization methods, box plots are a very clear and efficient way of visualizing distributions of a numerical variable for different groups.



12.2.4 Timelines
Finally, line graphs are preferred when one of the variable is a temporal unit (a date, a year, a day, etc.). In the example below, we observe the trend of the number of publications in the Canadian Journal of Administrative Sciences over four decades.

We can add multiple trends to in the same graph too. For example, the graph below shows the average number of institutions and countries listed on the publications in the journals, which indicate an increase in interinstitutional and international collaboration in the field over time.

title: 4  Finding and retrieving data
text:
4.2 Example types of data sources

4.2.1 Internal organizational data
When working for a company, public agency, nonprofit organization, or client, internal systems are often the first place to look. Organizations generate information through routine activities: customer relationship management systems, point-of-sale transactions, inventory systems, human-resource platforms, accounting systems, websites, mobile applications, service records, and operational databases. These data can be especially valuable because they are closely connected to the organization’s own decisions and processes. 
Internal data might describe clients, products, inventories, sales, employees, expenditures, financial performance, or interactions with services. However, “internal database” should not be imagined as a single clean table containing everything an analyst wants. Different organizational systems may have been created for different operational purposes. Customer identifiers may differ across systems; dates and categories may be encoded differently; access may be restricted; and data definitions may reflect administrative needs rather than analytical ones. 
The analyst should begin by understanding what systems exist, who is responsible for them, what each record represents, and what permissions are required. Retrieval may occur through a report export, a CSV or Excel download, a database query, a business-intelligence interface, or an API. The appropriate method depends on the organization and the system. Regardless of method, you should retrieve only the information needed for the defined purpose and preserve documentation about the source and extraction.


4.2.2 Open government data
Governments and public organizations make substantial amounts of information available through open-data programs. Canada’s Open Government site provides a search interface for information resources and datasets published by government institutions. The federal catalogue includes resources distributed in multiple formats, including CSV, XLSX and JSON on some records. Open government data can support questions involving the economy, public spending, regulation, transportation, the environment, businesses, communities, and many other management-relevant topics. 
At the provincial level, the Nova Scotia Government Open Data Portal is designed to make government data easier to access for individuals, businesses, and researchers. Its catalogue organizes datasets across subjects such as business and economy, government administration, social services, and nature and environment.
Statistics Canada deserves particular attention because it offers several retrieval mechanisms. Its developer documentation states that users can download complete data tables in CSV format with accompanying data and metadata, while its Web Data Service provides programmatic access to aggregate data and metadata. Statistics Canada also provides JSON and SDMX-based services for various uses. This means the same source can support a beginner downloading a table for Excel and a more advanced analyst building a reproducible workflow that retrieves selected observations through an API. 
Open data should not be confused with data that can be used without reading any conditions. Analysts should check the applicable licence, attribution requirements, and documentation. For example, the Nova Scotia Open Government Licence permits broad reuse subject to conditions including source acknowledgement and identifies exclusions such as personal information and third-party rights. Licensing is therefore part of responsible data retrieval, not an afterthought. 


4.2.3 International and municipal public data
Management questions often cross national boundaries. The World Bankprovides an important source for international development and economic indicators, while national and municipal governments maintain their own portals. In the United States, Data.gov acts as a federal open-data catalogue. At the local level, cities, public libraries, transit organizations, and other public bodies may publish datasets that are more granular than national statistics. 
The level of government or institution should match the question. National indicators are useful for country comparisons, but local business-location decisions may require municipal or neighbourhood data. Similarly, a public library may publish information about branches, usage, programs, or collections that supports questions about public services. The important lesson is that “government data” is not one source. It is an ecosystem of producers operating at different geographic and administrative levels. 


4.2.4 Research data repositories
Research data provide another important source. Open research practices encourage researchers to preserve and share datasets and other research outputs so that they can be discovered and reused. DataCite supports discovery by connecting research outputs and resources through DOI metadata. DataCite Commons provides an integrated interface for searching and filtering metadata, complemented by machine-actionable services such as a REST API and OAI-PMH. 
General-purpose repositories are useful when data are not housed in a discipline-specific archive. Zenodo describes itself as a general-purpose research repository in which users can share and preserve research outputs including data, software, publications, and presentations. Zenodo also recommends considering discipline-specific repositories where appropriate. Figshare similarly supports storing, sharing, and discovering research outputs and explicitly presents itself as a repository for data and other scholarly materials. 
Research repositories can be especially useful when a journal article refers to a dataset that would be useful for a new analysis. However, it should not be assumed that publication in a repository automatically makes a dataset relevant or methodologically appropriate. The repository helps with discovery, preservation, metadata, and citation; the analyst still has to inspect the dataset’s documentation, methods, variables, licensing, and suitability for the new question. 


4.2.5 Miscellaneous public datasets and dataset search engines
The web contains many additional datasets. Kagglehosts datasets alongside analytics and machine-learning activities. The Awesome Public Datasets project on GitHub curates links across many topics. IMDb makes downloadable datasets available for non-commercial use through its interfaces page. Such sources can be valuable for practice, demonstrations, and particular research questions, but their authority, licensing, documentation, and provenance vary. A well-known hosting platform should not be mistaken for the original producer of every file hosted there. 
Google Dataset Search offers another discovery strategy. Instead of searching only ordinary webpages. This can is useful when the analyst knows the topic but not the repository. A dataset search engine is therefore complementary to curated library guides and dedicated government portals: the guide points to selected sources, the portal searches a known collection, and the search engine searches across many sources. 
Search strategy still matters. It can be helpful to combine substantive keywords with terms such as “dataset,” “data,” “CSV,” “XLSX,” “JSON,” “download,” “API,” or “open data”, or search within a known domain when they want a specific producer. The goal is to move from webpages discussing a phenomenon to records that expose the observations themselves or explain how to retrieve them. 


4.2.6 Library data guides and human expertise 
A web search is not always the fastest route. University libraries often provide data and statistics guides that organize major sources by subject, geography, or publisher. The Data and Statistics Guide from Dalhousie Libraries can serve as a curated starting point for locating statistical resources. Guides of this kind reduce the discovery problem by connecting users to credible repositories and explaining what kinds of data they contain. 
The value of a guide is not that it replaces searching. Rather, it narrows the search space. Investigating where to locate a coffee shop might begin with census and population resources, then identify business or trade data, and then supplement them with provincial or municipal sources. A librarian or data specialist can also help clarify whether a desired dataset exists, whether access is licensed, and how a particular interface works.

title: 4  Finding and retrieving data
text:
4.3 Recognizing the actual data 
One of the most common difficulties for beginning analysts is distinguishing a webpage about data from the data themselves. A news release, chart, dashboard, report, or landing page may summarize information without exposing the underlying observations in a form that can be analyzed.
File formats provide clues about how retrieval will work. CSV is a simple tabular text format that can be opened in spreadsheet applications. XLSX is an Excel workbook and may contain multiple sheets, formatting, formulas, or metadata. JSON is a structured text format frequently used by APIs and can contain nested objects and lists rather than a flat table. API access allows software to request selected records or fields programmatically. More specialized sources may also offer XML, SDMX, GIS formats, or database access. 
Format choice should reflect the task. A small one-time analysis may be easiest with a CSV or Excel download. A project that must update regularly may benefit from an API. A large table may be better retrieved selectively rather than downloaded in full. The analyst should also obtain metadata or data dictionaries whenever available, because variables without definitions can be difficult to interpret correctly.

title: 4  Finding and retrieving data
section: 4.4 From downloading to querying: methods of retrieval
text:
4.4 From downloading to querying: methods of retrieval
Downloading a file is the most visible form of retrieval, but there are several common methods.
The first is direct file download, often as CSV, XLSX, JSON, or a compressed archive.
The second is database querying. In a relational database, a query can select particular columns, filter rows, join tables, and aggregate results. Even managers who do not become database specialists benefit from understanding that a query is a precise request for a subset of stored data. 
The third method is an API. An API allows an application to request information from a service in a structured way. Statistics Canada, for example, describes its Web Data Service as a mechanism for accessing aggregate data and metadata directly from its public databases and documents JSON-based methods. API retrieval can make an analysis reproducible because the selection logic can be recorded in code, but it also requires attention to documentation, authentication, usage conditions, pagination, and changing service requirements. 
The fourth method is specialized search or export software. Some systems provide built-in exports; other services are accessed through packages in R or Python. The general principle is to choose the simplest method that reliably retrieves the observations needed while preserving enough metadata to understand them.
